questions.prompt: Describe what the vowel scatterplot shows and how it relates to the network’s inputs and targets.
questions.answer: Each of the 525 dots is one vowel token placed by its F1 along the horizontal axis and F2 along the vertical axis, in hertz. The color gives its correct word. The positions are the network’s two inputs, and the colors are the targets it is trained to match.
rubric: Identify F1, F2 and color correctly.
Connect positions to inputs and colors to targets.

questions.prompt: Explain why i and ae are easier to identify from F1 and F2 than u, a and schwa.
questions.answer: i sits high on F2, mostly above about 2000 Hz, and ae reaches high F1 values, so their positions set them apart. u, a and schwa crowd into the same lower-middle region, so a token there could belong to any of the three.
rubric: State where i and ae fall.
Describe the shared region of u, a and schwa.

questions.prompt: Explain why overlapping vowel clouds set an upper limit on any classifier that uses only F1 and F2.
questions.answer: The classifier sees only F1 and F2. Tokens with different labels that land in the same place give it the same input, so whichever word it chooses for that input, some of those tokens are labeled wrong.
rubric: Explain that equal inputs get the same response.
Conclude that some overlapping tokens must be wrong.

questions.prompt: Use the 105 tokens per vowel to explain the 20% starting level of the accuracy curve.
questions.answer: Each vowel has 105 of the 525 tokens. A network that labels every token with the same word gets that vowel’s 105 tokens right, which is one fifth, or 20%.
rubric: Use 105 of 525.
Connect equal class sizes to the one-in-five level.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of torch.manual_seed(0) in the one-initialization program.
questions.answer: The seed fixes the random starting weights, so the run starts from one particular initialization and can be repeated exactly. It does not change the data, the loss or the learning rate.
rubric: Link the seed to the starting weights.
Distinguish it from the other training settings.

questions.prompt: Explain why the program divides the formants by 1000 before training.
questions.answer: Raw formants are hundreds or thousands of hertz, much larger than the other values in the network. Dividing by 1000 gives kilohertz values that keep the inputs small, so the input weights are not pushed by very large numbers.
rubric: State the unit change.
Explain why smaller inputs help training.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens in one epoch of the training loop, in order.
questions.answer: opt.zero_grad() clears old gradients. loss_fn(model(X), TrueVowel_Outputs) runs the forward pass and computes cross-entropy on all tokens. loss.backward() computes the gradients. opt.step() updates the weights once.
rubric: Give the four calls in order.
State that one epoch is one full-batch update.

questions.prompt: Explain how the program turns the network’s scores into an accuracy percentage.
questions.answer: For each token, argmax picks the word with the largest score. The program compares those answers with the correct classes, takes the fraction that match, and multiplies by 100 to save a percentage.
rubric: Mention the largest score as the answer.
Describe the comparison and percentage.

questions.prompt: Describe the shape of the one-initialization accuracy curve and its final value.
questions.answer: Accuracy stays near 20% for about the first 200 updates, then climbs into the 40s. It dips sharply near update 390, recovers, and is essentially flat after about 450 updates, ending at 44.95%, or 236 of 525 tokens.
rubric: Describe the flat start and rise.
Give the final value.

questions.prompt: Explain why the curve reports training accuracy and what it does not tell us.
questions.answer: Accuracy is measured on the same 525 tokens the network learns from. It shows how well the network fits those tokens, but it does not show how it would label new recordings it has never seen.
rubric: Identify the tokens used for measurement.
State what remains unknown.

questions.prompt: Explain how to interpret a PyTorch program shown next to a curve made with NumPy.
questions.answer: PyTorch was unavailable where the plot was made, so the same network, loss, scaling, learning rate and number of updates were run in NumPy. The code describes the procedure, and the curve is the measured result of running that procedure in an equivalent implementation.
rubric: Give the reason for NumPy.
State that the procedure is the same.

questions.prompt: Explain what is held constant and what is varied across the ten training runs.
questions.answer: Each run uses a fresh model and optimizer with the same data, scaling, loss, learning rate and 2,000 full-batch updates. Only the seed, and so the starting weights, changes, so differences between runs come from initialization.
rubric: List what stays the same.
Identify initialization as the only change.

questions.prompt: Describe how the ten curves differ in the early part of training.
questions.answer: All start near 20%, but some leave that level within 100 updates while others stay flat for 200 or more. Some dip back toward 20% before recovering, and their peaks along the way differ, reaching close to 47% in some runs.
rubric: Describe differences in timing.
Mention dips or peaks.

questions.prompt: Explain what the shared 44.95% end point suggests about where the accuracy limit comes from.
questions.answer: Every initialization ends at the same accuracy, so the starting weights affect only the path. The limit comes from the network and the data, including the overlapping vowel clouds, rather than from an unlucky start.
rubric: Link the shared value to initialization not mattering at the end.
Name the network and data as the limit.

questions.prompt: Explain why equal seed numbers in NumPy and PyTorch do not give equal starting weights.
questions.answer: Each library has its own random-number stream, so the same seed number produces different starting weights. A PyTorch run with a given seed would follow a somewhat different path, even though the overall pattern of varied paths and a common end could still appear.
rubric: Explain separate random streams.
State the consequence for individual curves.

questions.prompt: Connect the overlap in the vowel scatterplot to the accuracy ceiling across ten seeds.
questions.answer: Many tokens of u, a and schwa share the same F1–F2 region. A network that sees only these two numbers cannot label all of them correctly, so every run, whatever its starting weights, levels off well below 100%.
rubric: Use the overlapping region.
Link it to the shared ceiling.

questions.prompt: Explain how the listed output logits become the five displayed probabilities.
questions.answer: Softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum of all five exponentials. The largest logit, 0.622 for done, becomes the largest probability, 55.7%, and the probabilities add to one.
rubric: Describe exponentiation and normalization.
Match the largest logit to done.

questions.prompt: For the 320, 2000 recording, explain how the computed output and desired output are compared during backpropagation.
questions.answer: The computed output is the network’s probabilities, with done highest at 55.7%. The desired output puts 1 at dean and 0 elsewhere. Cross-entropy uses the 8.1% given to dean, and backpropagation finds how each weight affects that loss.
rubric: Name the favored word and the target.
Connect the target probability to the loss.

questions.prompt: Predict whether increasing the pink-marked weight into done raises or lowers the error for a dean target, and explain.
questions.answer: The error goes up. The weight carries a positive hidden value into done, so done’s score rises. Softmax shares one total, so dean’s probability falls and the cross-entropy loss increases.
rubric: State that error rises.
Trace the effect through done and softmax.

questions.prompt: Explain why backpropagation works from the output toward the input and how that connects to dynamic programming.
questions.answer: The last weights affect the output directly, while earlier weights act through later layers. Computing the later effects first lets them be reused for earlier weights instead of recomputed, the same reuse of smaller results that dynamic programming uses.
rubric: Contrast direct and indirect effects.
Explain the reuse.

questions.prompt: Explain how the input and target matrices pair each recording with its answer, and note the count on the vowel plot.
questions.answer: Each row of the input matrix holds one recording’s F1 and F2, and the same row of the target matrix marks its correct word with a 1. The rows must stay in the same order. These matrices are labeled with 110 rows, while the vowel plot and training runs use 525 tokens.
rubric: Explain row pairing.
Mention the 110 and 525 labels.

questions.prompt: Compare the one-step PyTorch program with the 2,000-epoch training loop.
questions.answer: Both use the same network sizes, cross-entropy and SGD with learning rate 0.1. The one-step program updates once, while the loop repeats the update 2,000 times, scales the inputs, removes biases, and records accuracy after each step.
rubric: Name shared settings.
Name what the loop adds.

questions.prompt: Explain how sigmoid saturation relates to the description of neurons as nearly digital.
questions.answer: Large negative inner products give outputs near 0 and large positive ones give outputs near 1, such as 0.018 for −4 and 0.982 for 4. At the flat ends the output barely changes, so the neuron behaves almost like it is off or on, while the middle stays graded.
rubric: Use near-0 and near-1 behavior.
Connect it to nearly digital.

questions.prompt: Explain why Dan becoming the most probable word after adding sigmoid is not learning.
questions.answer: The formants and weights stay fixed, and only the hidden activation rule changes, so downstream values and the outputs change. The target is still dean, and no weights were updated, so the new favorite is not evidence of training.
rubric: State what stays fixed.
Distinguish an activation change from a weight update.

questions.prompt: Describe how the 2,000-epoch training code would change to train a network with hidden sigmoids.
questions.answer: Insert nn.Sigmoid() after each of the first three nn.Linear layers, leaving the final Linear(4, 5) to give logits to CrossEntropyLoss. The loop, scaling, loss and optimizer could stay the same.
rubric: Place sigmoid after the hidden layers.
Keep the final layer’s logits for the loss.
